In the foraging task of Clarke, Irons, James, Leber & Hunt (2022,
*QJEP*), 58 people selected all 40 targets on each trial, 20 of each of
two types, in a **feature** and a **conjunction** condition. As in other
foraging studies, people tend to collect one target type in long runs in
conjunction foraging, and switch more freely in feature foraging. The
paper's abstract says 64 people were tested; the data have 58 (exclusions,
still to be confirmed). With 87,760 selections it is the
largest dataset here.

This page shows how to work with a fitted model: checking convergence,
reading the posterior, accuracy and posterior predictive checks.
The model is the default one: multi-level, Fourier-124 directions, the
default priors, 4 chains of 1000 warmup and 1000 sampling iterations.

*Note*: this page doesn't fit anything. It reads a saved fit
(`clarke2022qjep_fourier124.rds`) from `fits/` in this folder.
It isn't in the repository: to make it, run `fit_clarke2022qjep.R` in this
folder (about 4 hours on a laptop), which saves it there. See
`examples/real_data/README.md`.

Code: `clarke2022qjep.R`.

```{r}
#| include: false
knitr::read_chunk("clarke2022qjep.R")
```

```{r load}
```

## The fit

```{r read-fit}
```

Population-level estimates (medians and 97% HPDIs) and convergence.
R-hat and ESS are coloured green (good), orange (acceptable) or red
(bad). At 1000 iterations this fit's largest R-hat is 1.02 and its smallest
bulk ESS about 200: fine for a walkthrough, but a published analysis
should use 2000.

```{r fit-summary}
#| results: asis
```

Rank plots of the five worst-mixing parameters. If the chains have mixed
well, each chain's histogram is roughly flat and they overlap.

```{r fig-traces}
#| fig-height: 2.2
#| fig-cap: "Rank plots of the five worst-mixing parameters, coloured by their R-hat and ESS."
```

## Posterior

`extract_post()` turns the fit's draws into tidy tables (one per group of
parameters), which the `plot_post_*()` functions take.

```{r extract}
#| cache: true
#| cache.extra: !expr list(file.mtime("fits/clarke2022qjep_fourier124.rds"), rlang::hash(d))
```

```{r fig-post}
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "Posterior densities by condition: class transitions, distance and relative direction, and the Fourier coefficients. Grey bands: the priors' HPDIs."
```

The same spatial parameters, shown as what each does to an item's
selection weight:

```{r fig-post-weights}
#| fig-cap: "Relative selection weight against distance, turn and absolute direction: 53% and 97% HPDIs."
```

Each person's distance and relative-direction estimates, over the
population's:

```{r fig-person}
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "Per-person estimates (intervals) over the population-level HPDIs (grey bands)."
```

And each person's class-transition probabilities: how likely they are to
select each target type next, given the type they just selected. With two
types each row of the matrix sums to one, so the columns come in mirrored
pairs.

```{r fig-person-cat}
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "Per-person class-transition probabilities (previous type -> next type) over the population-level HPDIs (grey bands)."
```

## Accuracy

The fit doesn't store a prediction for every selection
(`save_selections = FALSE`, the default), so `predict_fomo()` makes them
from 200 posterior draws. Deterministic accuracy is how often the item the
model judges most likely is the one selected; the probability of the
chosen item credits being nearly right too. Chance (dotted) is
1 / items left; the nearest-neighbour rule (dashed) always picks the
closest item, so the gap above it is what the model adds to proximity
alone. This is in-sample accuracy, which overestimates out-of-sample
accuracy.

```{r predict}
#| cache: true
#| cache.extra: !expr list(file.mtime("fits/clarke2022qjep_fourier124.rds"), rlang::hash(d))
```

```{r fig-accuracy}
#| fig-cap: "Accuracy at each selection, with chance and nearest-neighbour baselines."
```

## Posterior predictive check

Whole trials simulated from the fitted model (5 posterior draws: the
dataset is large), compared with the data. The
model doesn't predict when a trial stops, so each simulated trial keeps as
many selections as the observed one.

```{r sim-posterior}
#| cache: true
#| cache.extra: !expr list(file.mtime("fits/clarke2022qjep_fourier124.rds"), rlang::hash(d), n_post_draws)
```

```{r fig-sim-trial}
#| fig-cap: "One trial per condition, simulated from the fitted model."
```

```{r fig-sim-stats}
#| cache: true
#| cache.extra: !expr rlang::hash(list(found_post, trial_stats))
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Trial statistics for the data (x) and simulated from the posterior (y). Points near the diagonal mean the model reproduces them."
```
